**Audience**: an engineer who has trained a classifier / network and wants to move from *predicting* to *deciding* (recommendation, pricing, agents). **Empirical first**: Q-learning on a gridworld that stalls because ε-greedy is too low; DQN that diverges when the replay buffer leaks the distribution; then we name MDP, TD, policy gradient, RLHF.

From MDPs to dynamic programming, deep RL and LLM agents. Mandatory P2 module: the glue between supervision and LLM alignment ([LLMs](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) in M2).

::: def
[RLHF in three lines]{.tag} **Reinforcement learning from human feedback** (Ouyang et al., 2022) aligns a language model $\pi_\theta$ in three steps.

1.  Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations gives the reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.
2.  A reward model $r_\phi(x, y)$ is fitted to human comparisons $y_w \succ y_l$ by the Bradley–Terry likelihood (section 6.5).
3.  The policy maximizes $r_\phi$ minus the penalty $\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$ with PPO (Theorem 5.5); the optimum of this objective is given by the lemma that opens chapter 6.

The derivations, DPO and GRPO are in [Large Language Models, ch. 5](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch5).
:::

### What you will be able to do

-   Formalize a sequential problem as a Markov decision process: states, actions, transitions, rewards, policy.
-   Solve a known MDP by dynamic programming (value iteration, policy iteration).
-   Implement model-free learning methods: TD, SARSA, Q-learning.
-   Write policy gradient algorithms and actor-critic variants.
-   Carry out deep RL: DQN, Rainbow, DDPG/SAC, and offline learning (offline RL).
-   Master the exploration/exploitation trade-off, in particular in the bandit setting, and plan with Monte-Carlo tree search.
-   Represent uncertain knowledge with a Bayesian network and take a single-step decision by maximum expected utility.
-   Optimize policies without gradients (CEM, evolution strategies) and place a problem among the stochastic, multi-objective and constrained settings.
-   Explain and compare distributional, model-based, imitation/inverse and sequence-modeling (decision transformer) approaches.
-   Analyze autonomous agents in the era of LLMs: tool use, LLM agents, multi-agent systems, read as POMDPs and Markov games.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

The official 2026–2027 sheet (X3A session "Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents", period X-3A-P2, from 04/01/2027 to 19/03/2027, taught in English) presents a course on the *development of autonomous agents*: systems that perceive, learn and act independently to achieve goals in uncertain and dynamic environments, drawing on probabilistic decision-making, inference and planning.

It develops Markov decision processes and their key concepts, deep Q-learning and its variants, the policy gradient and actor-critic architectures, then model-based learning, gradient-free optimization, imitation learning and other routes to sequential decision-making such as model-based control and decision transformers, and the specialized topics of offline RL, distributional RL, imitation and inverse reinforcement learning — with an emphasis on modern deep architectures that scale, on the practical consequences of architectural and algorithmic choices, and on formulating decision problems well. Students implement, study and compare algorithms in several settings.

Official prerequisites: a course such as Machine Learning and/or Deep Learning and the associated concepts, plus Python and its scientific libraries.

Assessment: the LLGA section of the sheet displays none; the description announces a course project (50%) and practical work (50%), and the other programs list homework (50%) and a project (50%, oral).

::: note
[Team project (proposal)]{.tag} We propose to run the course project (50%) as the RL work package of the Year 1 team project: **one repository, three graded work packages**. The graph package is graded as the [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html) team project, the RL package as this course's project, and the NLP package as the [Text Mining and NLP](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html) capstone. The RL package of each Year 1 subject of the [end-of-year projects](../../projects/index.html) page:

-   **Y1.1** GraphRAG with a learned retrieval router: LinUCB (Algorithm 4.5) chooses the retrieval mode per question.
-   **Y1.2** fleet dispatch: a constrained MDP (Definition 6.5) solved by tabular Q-learning, then DQN or PPO.
-   **Y1.3** cold-start news recommendation: Thompson sampling and LinUCB (chapter 4) under drift.
-   **Y1.4** molecules from words: REINFORCE or PPO fine-tuning with a KL anchor (chapters 5–6) and a reward-hacking check.
-   **Y1.5** scene-graph question answering: a REINFORCE walker in a POMDP (Definition 7.1).

Solo and group variants, an exam proposal and a rubric are in [Projects and assessment](#projects).
:::

### Course outline

-   **Refresher and probabilistic reasoning** — Markov chains, martingales, dynamic programming, then Bayesian networks and single-step decisions by inference (official block 1).
-   **Markov decision processes** — the formal framework: agent, environment, policy, value function.
-   **Dynamic programming** — solving a known MDP: value and policy iterations.
-   **Learning: TD, SARSA, Q-learning** — learning without a model of the environment, by interaction.
-   **Bandits, exploration and Monte-Carlo tree search** — the exploration/exploitation trade-off in the simplest setting, then MCTS, where every tree node is a bandit.
-   **Policy gradients, actor-critic and gradient-free search** — differentiating the policy to optimize it directly, or optimizing it as a black box (CEM, evolution strategies, multi-objective settings, architecture search).
-   **Deep RL and advanced methods** — DQN, Rainbow and prioritized replay, DDPG/SAC, offline and safe RL, distributional RL, model-based RL and MPC, imitation and inverse RL, decision transformers.
-   **Autonomous agents in the era of LLMs** — tool use, LLM agents, Markov games and multi-agent learning: where RL meets language models.
-   **Course research notes (Jesse Read)** — a tour of the instructor's research work (self-study).
-   **Exercises**, **Projects and assessment** and **References** — systematic training, project subjects with an exam proposal, and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Assimilate the refresher section before anything else: without Markov chains or dynamic programming, MDPs and TD-learning remain opaque recipes.
-   Implement each algorithm on a small environment (gridworld, bandits): in RL, one only truly understands by coding the agent-environment loop.
-   Always plot learning curves over several random seeds: the variance of runs is in itself a lesson of the module.
-   Classify the algorithms by their assumptions — on-policy or off-policy, online or offline, value or policy: this mental table is worth more than any mnemonic device.
-   Read the section on LLM agents early, even though it comes at the end of the course: it gives a concrete and modern motivation for everything that precedes it.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; the classic pitfalls (insufficient exploration, divergence of the critic) are encountered there first.

::: note
[Notation]{.tag} [Site-wide conventions](../../notation/index.html) for RL and RLHF, followed on this page:

-   MDP $(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r, \gamma)$; returns $G_t$ and $G(\tau)$; values $V^\pi$, $Q^\pi$ and advantage $A^\pi$.
-   Discounted occupancy $d^\pi$ (Definition 1.4); importance ratio $\rho_t(\theta)$; Fisher matrix $F(\theta)$.
-   RLHF: policy $\pi_\theta$, reference $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$, reward model $r_\phi(x, y)$, preferences $y_w \succ y_l$, KL coefficient $\beta$.
-   Bandit index $\mathrm{UCB}_a(t)$, with UCT written in the same form.

**Deviations on this page:**

-   TD, Q-learning and actor-critic steps are written $\alpha$, as in Sutton & Barto; the generic learning rate $\eta$ is kept for Robbins–Monro (Theorem 0.5).
-   $\alpha$ is also the temperature of SAC and the width of the LinUCB bonus (Algorithm 4.5).
-   $\pi$ is a stationary distribution in the Markov-chain recap of chapter 0, and a tour in section 5.5, as in Kool et al. (2019).
:::

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} Reinforcement learning is the glue between the two axes of the master's program: it is through it that LLMs get aligned (RLHF) and that agents are deployed on graph-structured environments. Careers in sequential decision-making — recommendation, pricing, robotics, games — and research on the alignment of generative models all mobilize these methods, and the [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) module (M2) makes immediate use of them.
:::

## 0. Refresher and probabilistic reasoning: Markov chains, Bayesian networks, dynamic programming {#ch0}

Reinforcement learning algorithms are random processes that try to reach the fixed point of an equation. Proving that they work takes three tools, recalled in this chapter: Markov chains (the trajectory of an agent with a fixed policy is one), stochastic approximation (learning from noisy updates), and dynamic programming (the recursive structure of optimal decisions). Section 0.4 then adds the first block of the official programme: representing uncertain knowledge with a Bayesian network and taking a single decision by inference.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 prerequisites — Markov chains
:::

-   **Markov chain**: $X_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid X_t)$ — the future depends only on the present. Stochastic transition matrix (rows summing to 1).
-   **Stationary distribution**: $\pi = \pi P$; exists and is unique for an irreducible aperiodic chain (Perron-Frobenius theorem).
-   **Random walks on graphs**: $P = D^{-1}A$ — the random walker; $\pi(v) \propto \deg(v)$; to be connected to PageRank and node embeddings (Graph ML module).
-   **Conditional expectation**: $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$ (cf. Refresher Statistics module) — the value function is one.
::::

### 0.1. Classification of states, ergodicity

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Irreducibility, aperiodicity, recurrence]{.tag} A chain on $\mathcal{S}$ is **irreducible** if for all $i, j$ there exists $t$ with $P^t(i, j) > 0$ (every state is reachable from every state). It is **aperiodic** if the gcd of the return times to each state equals 1. A state is **positive recurrent** if the expected return time $\mathbb{E}[T_{i \to i}]$ is finite. An irreducible, aperiodic, positive recurrent chain is called **ergodic**.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Ergodic theorem for Markov chains]{.tag} Let $(X_t)$ be an ergodic chain with stationary distribution $\pi$. Then, for every bounded function $f : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}$, $$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} f(X_t) \;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\; \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \pi(s)\, f(s),$$ and moreover $\|P^t(i, \cdot) - \pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \to 0$ at geometric speed (for a finite chain, the rate is the modulus of the second largest eigenvalue of $P$).

*RL reading: in the long run, the visit frequency of a state does not depend on the initial state — this is what justifies learning "over the course of episodes".*
:::

### 0.2. Martingales and stochastic approximation

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Martingale]{.tag} $(M_t)$ is a martingale adapted to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ if $\mathbb{E}[M_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = M_t$. Martingales model "fair noise"; the TD error of chapter 3 will be almost one.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.4 — Robbins-Siegmund (quasi-martingale convergence)]{.tag} Let $V_t \geq 0$ be adapted, with $\mathbb{E}[V_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] \leq V_t + a_t$ where $\sum_t a_t < \infty$. Then $V_t$ converges a.s. to a finite random variable.

This is the central tool of the convergence proofs of this course's algorithms: one shows that the distance to the fixed point decreases "on average", and one concludes.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Robbins-Monro (precise statement)]{.tag} Consider the recursion
$$
x_{t+1} = x_t + \eta_{t+1}\big(h(x_t) + \xi_{t+1}\big),
$$
where $h : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is continuous, $x^\star$ the unique zero of $h$, and:

-   **(i)** steps $\sum_t \eta_t = \infty$, $\sum_t \eta_t^2 < \infty$;
-   **(ii)** unbiased noise $\mathbb{E}[\xi_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = 0$;
-   **(iii)** $(x_t - x^\star)^\top\big(h(x_t)\big) < 0$ as soon as $x_t \neq x^\star$ (monotonicity);
-   **(iv)** at most linear growth of the drift and of the noise: for a constant $C$,
    $$
    \|h(x_t)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\big[\|\xi_{t+1}\|^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_t\big] \leq C\big(1 + \|x_t\|^2\big).
    $$

Then
$$
x_t \to x^\star \quad \text{a.s.}
$$

Condition (iv) cannot be dropped. With $h(x) = -x^3$, which satisfies (iii), a start $x_0 = 10$ and $\eta_1 = 1$, the first step lands at $x_1 = -990$, and the following steps overshoot further and further: the iterates diverge.

*This is exactly the regime of TD-learning: $h$ will be the Bellman operator minus the identity, and Theorem 0.4 will provide the decrease.*
:::

### 0.3. Deterministic dynamic programming

::: prop
[Principle of optimality (Bellman, 1957)]{.tag} "An optimal policy has the property that, whatever the initial state and the first decision, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision." Formally, for a sequential additive cost, the optimal value satisfies a fixed-point equation:
$$
V^\star(x) = \min_u\{c(x, u) + V^\star(\mathrm{succ}(x, u))\}.
$$

Usage reminders: shortest paths (Bellman-Ford), memoization (Refresher CS), temporal decomposition. The MDP of chapter 1 adds: *random* transitions (hence expectations) and a maximization (hence $\max$ operators).
:::

### 0.4. Probabilistic reasoning: Bayesian networks and decisions as inference

This section is the first block of the official programme: before any sequence of decisions, an agent must represent what it knows about an uncertain world and choose *one* action well. A Bayesian network is the standard way to write that knowledge down, and the single-step decision rule it supports — maximize expected utility under the posterior — is exactly what the Bellman equations of chapter 1 will repeat over time.

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Bayesian network]{.tag} A **Bayesian network** over random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$ is a directed acyclic graph $G$ together with one conditional distribution per node given its parents $\mathrm{pa}(i)$. The joint distribution factorizes along the graph:
$$
p(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p\big(x_i \mid x_{\mathrm{pa}(i)}\big).
$$

The graph encodes conditional independences: each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents (local Markov property).

The gain is compactness: $n$ binary variables with at most $k$ parents each need $n\,2^k$ numbers instead of the $2^n - 1$ of an unstructured table.

A Markov chain is the simplest Bayesian network (a path $X_0 \to X_1 \to \dots$), and an MDP trajectory is one too, with the actions as extra nodes.
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Single-step decision: maximum expected utility]{.tag} Add to the network a **decision node** $A$, chosen by the agent, and a **utility** $U(x, a)$. Given observed evidence $e$, the rational action is
$$
a^\star \in \arg\max_a\ \mathbb{E}[U(X, a) \mid e, a] = \arg\max_a \sum_x p(x \mid e, a)\, U(x, a).
$$

Reasoning splits into two steps: *inference* (compute the posterior of the hidden variables given the evidence) and *decision* (maximize an expectation under that posterior).

With $U = r$ and a single time step, this is the bandit of chapter 4 with a known model; repeated over time with a state that evolves, it becomes the MDP of chapter 1.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.8 — The umbrella decision, computed]{.tag} Let $R$ = "it will rain" with prior $p(R) = 0.3$, and a forecast $F$ with $p(F = \text{rain} \mid R) = 0.8$, $p(F = \text{rain} \mid \neg R) = 0.1$ (network $R \to F$).

Utilities: take the umbrella and it rains, $0$; take it and it stays dry, $-1$; leave it and it rains, $-10$; leave it and it stays dry, $0$.

-   **Forecast "rain".** Bayes:
    $$
    p(R \mid F) = \frac{0.3 \cdot 0.8}{0.3 \cdot 0.8 + 0.7 \cdot 0.1} = \frac{0.24}{0.31} \approx 0.774 .
    $$
    Then $\mathbb{E}U(\text{take}) = -1 \cdot 0.226 = -0.226$ and $\mathbb{E}U(\text{leave}) = -10 \cdot 0.774 = -7.74$: take it.
-   **Forecast "dry".**
    $$
    p(R \mid \neg F) = \frac{0.3 \cdot 0.2}{0.3 \cdot 0.2 + 0.7 \cdot 0.9} = \frac{0.06}{0.69} \approx 0.087 ,
    $$
    so $\mathbb{E}U(\text{take}) \approx -0.913$ and $\mathbb{E}U(\text{leave}) \approx -0.87$: leave it, by a narrow margin.

The same network gives opposite actions depending on the evidence — the policy is a function of the observation, as it will be in every later chapter.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.9 — Approximate inference: importance sampling and sequential Monte-Carlo]{.tag} When the posterior cannot be summed exactly, it is sampled.

**Importance sampling**: for a proposal $q$ that covers the support of $p$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)] = \mathbb{E}_q\Big[f(X)\,\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\Big] \approx \frac{\sum_i w_i\, f(x_i)}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad x_i \sim q,\ \ w_i = \frac{p(x_i)}{q(x_i)},
$$
the self-normalized form being usable when $p$ is known only up to a constant (a posterior). Its reliability is measured by the effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS} = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$, which collapses toward $1$ when a few weights dominate.

**Sequential Monte-Carlo (particle filter)**: to track a hidden state $S_t$ from observations $O_t$, keep $N$ particles; at each step

1.  move each particle with the transition model, $s_t^i \sim P(\cdot \mid s_{t-1}^i, a_{t-1})$,
2.  weight it by the observation likelihood $w_t^i \propto \Omega(o_t \mid s_t^i, a_{t-1})$,
3.  then resample in proportion to the weights.

The particle cloud approximates the *belief* of a POMDP (Definition 7.1). The same importance ratio $p/q$ reappears as $\pi_\theta / \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}$ in off-policy learning and in PPO (Theorem 5.5).
:::

::: note
[Control as inference]{.tag} The two steps can be merged: attach to each time step a binary "optimality" variable $O_t$ with $p(O_t = 1 \mid s_t, a_t) \propto \exp(r(s_t, a_t))$ and condition the trajectory network on $O_t = 1$ for all $t$. The posterior over actions is then a softmax of soft Q-values — exactly the maximum-entropy policy of SAC (Algorithm 6.4; Levine, 2018). Planning becomes a probabilistic inference task, which is the viewpoint announced by the official programme for this first week.
:::

## 1. Markov decision processes {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a pricing agent updates its estimates $Q(s,a)$ online. After 10,000 episodes its learning curve rises; with another random seed the same code collapses, and the variance of the return is three times larger from one run to the next. Before any deep-learning trick, one must state precisely what is being optimized: this chapter sets up the Markov decision process.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Misspecified reward (the agent maximises the wrong thing); too little exploration (frozen policy); off-policy training without replay / target network (divergence). All three sabotage RLHF as much as a toy FrozenLake.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — MDP]{.tag} An **MDP** is a tuple
$$
(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, r, \gamma) :
$$
states $\mathcal{S}$, actions $\mathcal{A}$, transition kernel $P(s' \mid s, a)$, reward $r(s, a, s')$ (we write $r(s,a)$ for its expectation), discount factor $\gamma \in [0, 1)$.

A **policy** $\pi(a \mid s)$ governs the choice of actions; the objective is the discounted expected return
$$
J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t R_t\Big].
$$

Fixing a policy $\pi$ in an MDP *induces a Markov chain* with kernel
$$
P^\pi(s' \mid s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) P(s' \mid s, a)
$$
— chapter 0 applies literally; $\gamma < 1$ guarantees that all the sums converge.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Stationary deterministic policies]{.tag} It suffices to search among *deterministic* policies $\pi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{A}$ and *stationary* ones (not depending on $t$): for every mixed non-stationary policy, there exists a stationary deterministic policy with at least equal value in every state.

(Proof: backward induction on the horizon then $\gamma$-discounted limiting passage; see Puterman, 2005.) The search space is finite: $|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}$ candidates — too large for enumeration, hence chapters 2 and following.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Value functions]{.tag} $$V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_t \gamma^t R_t \,\Big|\, S_0 = s\Big], \qquad Q^\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_t \gamma^t R_t \,\Big|\, S_0 = s, A_0 = a\Big].$$ $V^\pi$ = "how much the state is worth"; $Q^\pi$ = "how much the state-action pair is worth". We have
$$
V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\, Q^\pi(s,a) \quad\text{and}\quad Q^\pi(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V^\pi(s').
$$
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Occupancy measures]{.tag} The (normalized, discounted) occupancy measure of $\pi$ (from $\mu_0$) is $$d^\pi(s, a) = (1 - \gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t\, \mathbb{P}_\pi[S_t = s, A_t = a], \qquad \text{so that} \qquad J(\pi) = \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_{s,a} d^\pi(s,a)\, r(s,a).$$

$d^\pi$ is a probability distribution over $\mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A}$; it describes "where the policy lives". Its state marginal
$$
d^\pi(s) = \sum_a d^\pi(s, a) = (1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t\, \mathbb{P}_\pi[S_t = s]
$$
is the **discounted state-visitation distribution**, and $d^\pi(s,a) = d^\pi(s)\,\pi(a \mid s)$. It is the natural bridge toward the LP formulation below and toward the importance ratios of chapter 5 (sampling under $\pi$, evaluating under $\pi'$).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Bellman equations (evaluation)]{.tag} $$Q^\pi(s, a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V^\pi(s'), \qquad V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a) V^\pi(s')\Big].$$ *This is dynamic programming applied to time: today's value = immediate gain + discounted value of tomorrow.*

Writing $T_\pi$ for the operator
$$
(T_\pi V)(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\big[r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a) V(s')\big],
$$
the equation rewrites as $V^\pi = T_\pi V^\pi$ — a *linear* system of $|\mathcal{S}|$ equations ($(I - \gamma P^\pi) V = r^\pi$, invertible since $\gamma < 1$).
:::

::::: thm
[Theorem 1.6 — Optimality: existence, uniqueness (complete proof)]{.tag} Consider the optimal Bellman operator $$(\mathcal{T}V)(s) = \max_a \Big\{ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V(s') \Big\}.$$ **(1) $\mathcal{T}$ is a contraction of modulus $\gamma$** on $(\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ (a complete space). Proof in two lemmas:

:::: proof
**Lemma (max-Lipschitz).** For all bounded families of reals $(u_a)_a$, $(v_a)_a$:
$$
|\max_a u_a - \max_a v_a| \leq \max_a |u_a - v_a| .
$$
Indeed, for every $a$, $u_a \leq v_a + \max_b |u_b - v_b|$, so $\max_a u_a \leq \max_a v_a + \max_b |u_b - v_b|$; exchanging the roles, $|\max_a u_a - \max_a v_a| \leq \max_b |u_b - v_b|$.

**Contraction.** For each $s$, setting $u_a = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a) V(s')$ and $v_a$ the analogue for $V'$:
$$
\big|(\mathcal{T}V)(s) - (\mathcal{T}V')(s)\big| \leq \max_a \gamma \Big|\sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a)\big(V(s') - V'(s')\big)\Big| \leq \gamma\, \|V - V'\|_\infty,
$$
since $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution. Taking the max over $s$:
$$
\|\mathcal{T}V - \mathcal{T}V'\|_\infty \leq \gamma \|V - V'\|_\infty .
$$

**(2) Fixed point.** By Banach's fixed-point theorem (L3 reminder: contraction on a complete space), $\mathcal{T}$ admits a unique fixed point $V^\star$, and $\mathcal{T}^k V \to V^\star$ for every starting $V$, at geometric speed $\gamma^k$. We set $Q^\star = r + \gamma P V^\star$, which satisfies

::: key
[Key result — Bellman optimality equation]{.tag}
$$
Q^\star(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, \max_{a'} Q^\star(s', a').
$$
:::

**(3) Optimal policy.** Let $\pi^\star$ be greedy for $V^\star$: $\pi^\star(s) \in \arg\max_a Q^\star(s,a)$. Then $T_{\pi^\star} V^\star = \mathcal{T}V^\star = V^\star$, so
$$
\|T_{\pi^\star}^k V^\star - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k \|T_{\pi^\star} V^\star - V^\star\|_\infty = 0
$$
for every $k$; in the limit $V^{\pi^\star} = V^\star$.

Hence $\pi^\star$ attains the supremum $\sup_\pi V^\pi$ in every state: it is an optimal stationary deterministic policy. [∎]{.qed}
::::
:::::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Linear (LP) formulation of MDPs]{.tag} Solving an MDP amounts to solving the (dual) linear program: $$\max_{\mu \geq 0}\ \sum_{s,a} \mu(s,a)\, r(s,a) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_a \mu(s', a) \;=\; \nu(s') + \gamma \sum_{s,a} P(s' \mid s, a)\, \mu(s,a) \ \ \forall s',$$ where $\nu$ is the initial distribution.

The variables $\mu$ are the occupancy measures $= d^\pi/(1-\gamma)$; the constraints are "flow equations" (what enters a state = initial distribution + what leaves it, discounted). An extreme optimal solution of the polytope is attained at a deterministic policy, and $\pi^\star(s) = \arg\max_a \mu^\star(s, a)$. Interest: LPs are solved in polynomial time (but polynomial in $|\mathcal{S}|\, |\mathcal{A}|$, quickly enormous); the dual viewpoint also sheds light on the linear approximation methods for the value.

The primal writes
$$
\min_V \sum_s \nu(s) V(s) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad V(s) \geq r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P V \quad \text{for all } (s, a)
$$
— the constraints are the Bellman inequalities.
:::

::: note
[Role of $\gamma$]{.tag} $\gamma$ discounts the future but also conditions the whole theory: contraction of modulus $\gamma$, error bounds in $1/(1-\gamma)$ (chapter 2), variance of the returns. When $\gamma \to 1$, one tends toward the average criterion $\lim_T \frac{1}{T}\sum_t R_t$ — related to the ergodic theorem 0.2 — but all the rates degrade: RL lives with this tension.
:::

## 2. Dynamic programming (known model) {#ch2}

When the transition kernel $P$ and the reward $r$ are known, the Bellman equations of ch. 1 can be solved by computation alone, without any interaction. This chapter gives the two classical algorithms, value iteration and policy iteration, with their convergence proofs: everything that follows is a sampled or approximated version of them.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — Value iteration: convergence demonstrated]{.tag} Repeat until convergence: $$V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \Big\{ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V_k(s')\Big\} \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T}V_k.$$

::: proof
For every $k$ (writing $V^\star = \mathcal{T}V^\star$): $$\|V_{k+1} - V^\star\|_\infty = \|\mathcal{T}V_k - \mathcal{T}V^\star\|_\infty \leq \gamma\, \|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \ \Rightarrow\ \|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k \|V_0 - V^\star\|_\infty.$$

The convergence is **geometric with ratio $\gamma$**: each iteration removes a factor $\gamma$ from the error.

*Exploitable stopping criterion.*
$$
\|V_{k+1} - V_k\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon \quad \text{implies} \quad \|V_{k+1} - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \frac{\gamma\,\varepsilon}{1-\gamma} .
$$
Indeed, by contraction and the triangle inequality,
$$
\|V_{k+1} - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \gamma\|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \gamma\big(\varepsilon + \|V_{k+1} - V^\star\|_\infty\big).
$$
The previous iterate only gets $\|V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon/(1-\gamma)$, so the algorithm returns $V_{k+1}$.

To guarantee an error $\delta$ on the returned value, a residual $\varepsilon = \delta(1-\gamma)/\gamma$ is needed — the factor $1/(1-\gamma)$ "amplifies" any approximation error. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Policy iteration: monotone improvement demonstrated]{.tag} Alternate:

-   **(i)** exact *evaluation* $V^{\pi_k} = T_{\pi_k} V^{\pi_k}$ (linear system);
-   **(ii)** greedy *improvement*
    $$
    \pi_{k+1}(s) \in \arg\max_a r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a) V^{\pi_k}(s'),
    $$
    that is, $\pi_{k+1}$ greedy for $V^{\pi_k}$.

::: proof
**Monotonicity.** First
$$
T_{\pi_{k+1}} V^{\pi_k} = \mathcal{T}V^{\pi_k} \geq V^{\pi_k}
$$
component by component (the max over the actions dominates the action played by $\pi_k$).

Next, $T_{\pi_{k+1}}$ is *monotone* ($U \geq V \Rightarrow T_{\pi} U \geq T_\pi V$, by positive linearity of the expectation), so by induction
$$
T_{\pi_{k+1}}^{j+1} V^{\pi_k} \geq T_{\pi_{k+1}}^{j} V^{\pi_k} \geq V^{\pi_k} ;
$$
in the limit
$$
V^{\pi_{k+1}} = \lim_j T_{\pi_{k+1}}^j V^{\pi_k} \geq V^{\pi_k} .
$$

**Finite termination.** If $V^{\pi_{k+1}} = V^{\pi_k}$, then
$$
\mathcal{T}V^{\pi_k} = T_{\pi_{k+1}} V^{\pi_k} = V^{\pi_k} :
$$
$V^{\pi_k}$ is a fixed point of $\mathcal{T}$, hence equal to $V^\star$ (uniqueness, Th. 1.6).

Since the value increases strictly at every non-terminal iteration and there is a finite number ($|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}$) of deterministic policies, the algorithm stops after a finite number of iterations on an optimal policy. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Value vs policy iteration — costs and trade-offs]{.tag} Value iteration: cheap iterations ($O(|\mathcal{S}|^2 |\mathcal{A}|)$) but very many; policy iteration: few iterations (often < 20) but each one requires solving a linear system ($O(|\mathcal{S}|^3)$). In practice on large $\mathcal{S}$: neither is exactly tractable — but all of modern RL is a "noisy and approximated" version of these two schemes.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Modified policy iteration and asynchronous dynamic programming]{.tag}

**Modified PI** (Puterman & Shin, 1978): replace the *exact* evaluation of $\pi_k$ by $m$ applications of $T_{\pi_k}$ (with $m$ small). $m = \infty$ gives back PI, small $m$ gets closer to VI; one interpolates the cost per iteration and the number of iterations — often the best compromise in practice.

**Asynchronous DP** (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis): update a freely chosen state $s$ (Gauss-Seidel, partial sweeps, priority to relevant states). Theorem: if every state is visited infinitely often, asynchronous DP converges to $V^\star$.

This is the gateway to RL: the algorithms of chapters 3, 5 and 6 are "sampled" asynchronous DPs, where the update is made on the state *actually visited*.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Propagation of approximation errors]{.tag} Suppose that at every iteration a bounded error sneaks in: $\tilde V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T}\tilde V_k + \varepsilon_k$, with $\|\varepsilon_k\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon$. Then $$\|\tilde V_k - V^\star\|_\infty \;\leq\; \gamma^k \|\tilde V_0 - V^\star\|_\infty \;+\; \frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.$$

::: proof
By recursion and contraction:
$$
\|\tilde V_{k+1} - V^\star\| \leq \gamma \|\tilde V_k - V^\star\| + \varepsilon,
$$
then by telescoping
$$
\|\tilde V_k - V^\star\| \leq \sum_{i<k} \gamma^i \varepsilon + \gamma^k \|\tilde V_0 - V^\star\|
$$
and geometric sum. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Major consequence for deep RL: any approximation error (network, sampling) is multiplied by $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. With $\gamma = 0.99$, a factor of 100: this is why approximating $V$ or $Q$ is difficult, and why the choice of $\gamma$ is a genuine design choice.*
::::

```python
import numpy as np

# 4x4 gridworld: states 0..15, actions 0..3 (up, down, left, right)
S, A, gamma = 16, 4, 0.95
goal = 15
P = np.zeros((S, A, S)); r = -np.ones((S, A))
def step(s, a):
    i, j = divmod(s, 4)
    di, dj = [(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)][a]
    return 4*min(max(i+di,0),3) + min(max(j+dj,0),3)
for s in range(S):
    for a in range(A):
        s2 = step(s, a)
        P[s, a, s2] = 1.0
        if s2 == goal or s == goal: r[s, a] = 0.0
r[goal] = 0.0

def T_op(V):                      # optimal Bellman operator
    return (r + gamma * (P @ V)).max(axis=1)

# --- Value iteration (th. 2.1) ---
V = np.zeros(S)
for _ in range(200):
    V_new = T_op(V)
    gap = np.abs(V_new - V).max()
    V = V_new                                   # keep V_{k+1}: the iterate the bound covers
    if gap < 1e-10: break                       # stopping criterion th. 2.1
Q = r + gamma * (P @ V)
print("VI :", V.reshape(4,4).round(2))

# --- Policy iteration (th. 2.2) ---
pi = np.zeros(S, dtype=int); V = np.zeros(S)
while True:
    # (i) exact evaluation: (I - gamma P^pi) V = r^pi
    R = r[np.arange(S), pi]
    Ppi = P[np.arange(S), pi]
    V = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(S) - gamma * Ppi, R)
    # (ii) greedy improvement
    Q = r + gamma * (P @ V)
    pi_new = Q.argmax(axis=1)
    if (pi_new == pi).all(): break              # stable policy: optimal
    pi = pi_new
print("PI :", V.reshape(4,4).round(2))
```

## 3. Learning: TD, SARSA, Q-learning (unknown model) {#ch3}

In practice we know neither $P$ nor $r$: we *interact*. **Temporal-difference learning** learns by correcting each prediction toward the observation:

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.1 — TD(0), SARSA, Q-learning]{.tag}

-   **TD(0)** (evaluation):
    $$
    V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)\big] ;
    $$
    the bracket is the **TD error** $\delta_t$.
-   **SARSA** (on-policy):
    $$
    Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) - Q(S_t,A_t)\big].
    $$
-   **Q-learning** (off-policy): $$Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(S_{t+1}, a') - Q(S_t, A_t)\Big].$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Convergence of TD(0) and Q-learning (sketch via Robbins-Monro)]{.tag} Under sufficient exploration (every pair $(s,a)$ visited infinitely often) and steps $\alpha_t(s,a) \in (0,1)$ with $\sum_t \alpha_t = \infty$, $\sum_t \alpha_t^2 < \infty$, almost surely
$$
V_t \to V^\pi \quad \text{and} \quad Q_t \to Q^\star
$$
(TD(0), Tsitsiklis 1994; Q-learning, Watkins & Dayan 1992).

::: proof
**TD(0) is a Robbins-Monro recursion.** The update writes $V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\,\delta_t$ with $\delta_t = r + \gamma V(S') - V(s)$. With $S_t$ and $V$ fixed, the expectation of $\delta_t$ over the action, the reward and $S_{t+1}$ equals
$$
r^\pi(S_t) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P^\pi(s'\mid S_t) V(s') - V(S_t) = (T_\pi V - V)(S_t)
$$
— the TD error is *unbiased noise around the Bellman residual*.

The target equation is therefore $h(V) = T_\pi V - V = 0$, whose unique zero is $V^\pi$ (Theorem 1.5). The remainder satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 0.5.

When the states are visited according to the stationary distribution $\mu_\pi$ of the chain $P^\pi$ (Theorem 0.2; not the discounted occupancy $d^\pi$ of Definition 1.4), the mean update is $D_\pi(T_\pi V - V)$ with $D_\pi = \mathrm{diag}(\mu_\pi)$. The drift and the TD error are affine in $V$ and the rewards are bounded, so the growth condition (iv) holds.

Moreover $T_\pi$ is a $\gamma$-contraction for the weighted norm $\|x\|_{D_\pi} = \sqrt{x^\top D_\pi x}$; this gives the monotonicity condition (iii):
$$
(V - V^\pi)^\top D_\pi (T_\pi V - V) \leq -(1-\gamma)\|V - V^\pi\|^2_{D_\pi} .
$$
Theorem 0.4 (Robbins-Siegmund) then concludes.

**Q-learning: same scheme with two extra ingredients.**

-   **(i)** the operator $\mathcal{T}$ (with max) remains a contraction of modulus $\gamma$ (Theorem 1.6);
-   **(ii)** the max introduces a bias *conditional on the sample*, but not asymptotically: in the limit, the argmax is stable and the iteration converges to the unique fixed point $Q^\star$.

Hence the result: Q-learning converges *whatever the exploration policy* (as long as it visits everything) — this is the off-policy property. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — n-step returns and eligibility traces]{.tag} The $n$-step return mixes bootstrapping and Monte-Carlo: $$G_t^{(n)} = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1} R_{t+n} + \gamma^{n} V(S_{t+n}).$$

**TD($\lambda$), "forward" view**: geometrically average the n-step returns: $$G_t^\lambda = (1-\lambda) \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \lambda^{n-1} G_t^{(n)}.$$

**"Backward" view**, implementable online with one *eligibility trace* per state: $$e_t(s) = \gamma \lambda\, e_{t-1}(s) + \mathbb{1}[S_t = s], \qquad V_{t+1}(s) = V_t(s) + \alpha\, \delta_t\, e_t(s) \quad \forall s.$$

The trace accumulates the states "responsible" for the current reward and fades as $(\gamma\lambda)^k$. *Equivalence theorem* (Sutton & Barto, ch. 12): for tabular evaluation with fixed steps, the two views realize the same cumulative update over an episode — equivalence stated here without proof.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — GAE: derivation of the generalized advantage estimator]{.tag} Set the TD error for the critic $V$: $\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)$. Then:

::: proof
**Step 1 (telescoping).** By immediate recursion, $$G_t^{(n)} - V(S_t) = \sum_{l=0}^{n-1} \gamma^l\, \delta_{t+l} \qquad (\text{n-step advantage, } A_t^{(n)}).$$

**Step 2 (geometric mixing).** The GAE estimator is the combination $(1-\lambda)\sum_n \lambda^{n-1} A_t^{(n)}$ — the same as TD($\lambda$) — and the telescoping propagates to the sum: $$\hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l\, \delta_{t+l}.$$

**Bias-variance reading.**

-   $\lambda = 0$ gives $\hat A_t = \delta_t$: one bootstrap step, strong bias (if $V$ is poor), low variance.
-   $\lambda = 1$ gives $\hat A_t = G_t - V(S_t)$: Monte-Carlo, no bootstrap bias, maximal variance.

GAE allows positioning oneself between the two — it is the standard estimator of the algorithms of chapters 5 and 6 (Schulman et al., 2016). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — Q-learning overestimation: the bias of the max, demonstrated]{.tag} For all real random variables $X, Y$ with finite expectations: $$\mathbb{E}[\max(X, Y)] \;\geq\; \max\big(\mathbb{E}[X], \mathbb{E}[Y]\big),$$ with *strict* inequality if and only if $X - Y$ changes sign with positive probability: $\mathbb{P}(X > Y) > 0$ and $\mathbb{P}(Y > X) > 0$.

$X \neq Y$ almost surely is not enough: with $X = 2$ and $Y$ uniform on $[0, 1]$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(X, Y)] = 2 = \max(\mathbb{E}X, \mathbb{E}Y).
$$

::: proof
We write $\max(x,y) = \tfrac12\big(x + y + |x - y|\big)$. The function $(x,y) \mapsto |x - y|$ is convex, so by Jensen $\mathbb{E}|X - Y| \geq |\mathbb{E}X - \mathbb{E}Y|$.

Hence:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(X,Y)] = \tfrac12\big(\mathbb{E}X + \mathbb{E}Y + \mathbb{E}|X-Y|\big) \geq \tfrac12\big(\mathbb{E}X + \mathbb{E}Y + |\mathbb{E}X - \mathbb{E}Y|\big) = \max(\mathbb{E}X, \mathbb{E}Y),
$$
strict if and only if $\mathbb{E}|X-Y| > |\mathbb{E}X - \mathbb{E}Y|$.

Write $Z = X - Y = Z^+ - Z^-$ with $Z^\pm \geq 0$. Then $\mathbb{E}|Z| - \mathbb{E}Z = 2\,\mathbb{E}[Z^-]$ and $\mathbb{E}|Z| + \mathbb{E}Z = 2\,\mathbb{E}[Z^+]$.

So $\mathbb{E}|Z| = |\mathbb{E}Z|$ exactly when $Z^- = 0$ a.s. or $Z^+ = 0$ a.s., that is, when $Z$ keeps one sign: the inequality is strict if and only if $X - Y$ takes both signs with positive probability.

Moreover
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(X,Y)] \leq \max(\mathbb{E}X, \mathbb{E}Y) + \tfrac12\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X - Y)^2]} :
$$
the bias grows with the *noise*. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Application:* the Q-learning target, $y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$, takes the expectation of a max of *noisy* Q-values (network, sampling): the max preferentially selects overestimates, and the bootstrap propagates the bias — hence systematically optimistic values and overexcited policies.
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.6 — Double Q-learning: the correction]{.tag} Maintain *two* independent estimators $Q_A, Q_B$ (each updated on half of the transitions, or randomly swapped), and **decouple selection and evaluation**: $$a^\star = \arg\max_a Q_A(s', a), \qquad y = r + \gamma\, Q_B(s', a^\star), \qquad Q_A(s,a) \leftarrow Q_A(s,a) + \alpha\big[y - Q_A(s,a)\big]$$ (and symmetrically by swapping $A \leftrightarrow B$).

Since $\mathbb{E}[Q_B(s', a^\star)]$ is taken *without* a max over the noise of $Q_B$, the positive bias of Theorem 3.5 disappears (the argmax is still computed on $Q_A$, but the evaluation no longer "picks the noise that suits it").

This is the tabular version of van Hasselt (2010); the deep version (Double DQN, chapter 6) uses the current network and the target network as the two estimators.
:::

::: def
[Exploration: $\varepsilon$-greedy policy]{.tag} With probability $\varepsilon$: random action; otherwise $\arg\max_a Q(s, a)$. Without exploration, the learning signal dies out; decreasing $\varepsilon$ is the standard setting — chapter 4 systematizes this choice.
:::

::: note
[The deadly triad]{.tag} Function approximation (networks) + bootstrapping (TD targets) + off-policy (Q-learning): combining the three can make the iteration *diverge* (Baird's counterexample, 1995). The convergence proof of Theorem 3.2 collapses as soon as the operator is no longer a contraction *within the approximation class*. The whole of chapter 6 is an art of living with this triad: replay, target networks, clipping, double Q.
:::

::: note
[Q-learning ≠ SARSA in one sentence]{.tag} Q-learning learns the optimal policy *whatever* the exploration policy (off-policy); SARSA evaluates the policy *actually* followed (including exploration) — more cautious near cliffs! (Classic lab: Cliff Walking, exercise 3.)
:::

## 4. Bandits, exploration and Monte-Carlo tree search {#ch4}

Before learning in a world with many states, consider the simplest decision problem in which exploration matters: a single situation, several actions whose mean rewards are unknown, and a budget of $T$ trials. Every trial spent on a poor action is lost, yet without trying the actions one never learns which is best; this chapter measures that trade-off by the regret and gives the algorithms that handle it optimally.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — K-armed bandit]{.tag} An MDP with a single state: at each step choose an arm $a$ and receive $r \sim \nu_a$ (independent of the past). Objective: minimize the cumulative **regret**
$$
R_T = T\,\mu^\star - \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^T \mu_{A_t}\Big] = \sum_{a : \Delta_a > 0} \Delta_a\, \mathbb{E}[N_a(T)], \qquad \Delta_a = \mu^\star - \mu_a,
$$
where $N_a(T)$ counts the pulls of arm $a$.

The bandit isolates the exploration/exploitation trade-off without state generalization cost — and it is *already* a hard sequential problem: every datum received depends on the past action.
:::

::::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — UCB1: logarithmic regret, proof sketch]{.tag} **UCB1** (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer, 2002): play each arm once, then at each step play $A_t = \arg\max_a \mathrm{UCB}_a(t)$ with the index
$$
\mathrm{UCB}_a(t) = \hat\mu_a(t) + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_a(t)}}, \qquad c = \sqrt 2 \ \text{for UCB1}
$$
("optimism in the face of uncertainty": the bonus decreases in $1/\sqrt{N_a}$).

For rewards in $[0,1]$:

::: key
[Key result — UCB1 regret]{.tag}
$$
R_T \;\leq\; \sum_{a \neq a^\star} \frac{8 \log T}{\Delta_a} + \Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2}{3}\Big) \sum_a \Delta_a.
$$
:::

::: proof
1.  **Concentration (Hoeffding).** For an arm $a$ pulled $n$ times,
    $$
    \mathbb{P}\big(\hat\mu_a \leq \mu_a - u\big) \leq e^{-2 n u^2}
    $$
    — the empirical means concentrate around the true mean.
2.  **Optimism is reliable.** With $u = \sqrt{2\log t / N_a}$, the event "$\hat\mu_a + u < \mu_a$" (pessimistic index) has probability $\leq t^{-4}$ for each value of the pull count. The two bad events (optimal arm underestimated, arm $a$ overestimated) are union-bounded over the pull counts $s, s' \leq t$, then over $t$:
    $$
    \sum_{t \geq 1} 2\, t^2\, t^{-4} = 2 \sum_{t \geq 1} t^{-2} = \frac{\pi^2}{3},
    $$
    which is the $\pi^2/3$ term.

    Outside rare events, *the index always upper-bounds the true mean, so the optimal arm has an index $\geq \mu^\star$ and a suboptimal arm can only be chosen if its estimate is too high*.
3.  **Counting bad choices.** If $a \neq a^\star$ is chosen at time $t$, then (indices compared)
    $$
    \hat\mu_a + \sqrt{2\log t / N_a} \geq \hat\mu_{a^\star} + \sqrt{2\log t/N_{a^\star}} \geq \mu^\star,
    $$
    hence $\hat\mu_a \geq \mu^\star - \sqrt{2\log t/N_a}$ — but $\hat\mu_a \leq \mu_a + \sqrt{2\log t/N_a}$ outside rare events. Combining,
    $$
    N_a(t) \leq 8 \log T / \Delta_a^2
    $$
    before the arm is definitively dominated.
4.  **Regret.** Inject into $R_T = \sum_a \Delta_a \mathbb{E}[N_a(T)]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
:::::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Lai-Robbins lower bound (1985)]{.tag} For every *consistent* strategy (regret sub-polynomial in $T$ on all instances): $$\liminf_{T \to \infty} \frac{R_T}{\log T} \;\geq\; \sum_{a : \Delta_a > 0} \frac{\Delta_a}{\mathrm{KL}(\nu_a \,\|\, \nu_{a^\star})}.$$

Interpretation: distinguishing $\nu_a$ from $\nu_{a^\star}$ requires $\Omega(\mathrm{KL}^{-1} \log T)$ samples — information-theoretically. UCB1 loses at most a constant factor against this bound; optimized indices (KL-UCB) and Thompson sampling attain it asymptotically. *Regret in $\Theta(\log T)$ is therefore the law of the problem.*
:::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 4.4 — Thompson sampling: derived posteriors]{.tag} Maintain a posterior over each $\mu_a$; at each step, sample $\tilde\mu_a$ from each posterior and play $\arg\max_a \tilde\mu_a$. Pulls of a dominated arm naturally become rare: exploration emerges from the algorithm.

::: proof
**Bernoulli case: Beta conjugation.** Prior $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ of density $\propto \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}$, likelihood $\theta^{S}(1-\theta)^{F}$ ($S$ successes, $F$ failures).

The posterior is $\propto \theta^{\alpha + S - 1}(1-\theta)^{\beta + F - 1}$, that is, $$\mu_a \mid \text{data} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha + S_a,\ \beta + F_a)$$ — the update is a simple counting (uniform prior: $\alpha = \beta = 1$).

**Gaussian case: completing the square.** Rewards $\mathcal{N}(\mu_a, \sigma^2)$, prior $\mu_a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The posterior is Gaussian: $$v_n = \Big(\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\Big)^{-1}, \qquad m_n = v_n\, \frac{n\, \bar r}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \mu_a \mid \text{data} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_n, v_n)\,: $$ precisions (inverses of the variances) add up — one recovers the empirical estimator in the limit $n \to \infty$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Thompson sampling attains the Lai-Robbins bound (asymptotically, exponential families) and empirically dominates UCB — it is the industrial choice (recommendation, A/B tests). Chapelle & Li (2011) for the reference empirical study.
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.5 — Linear contextual bandits: LinUCB]{.tag} Context $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (user, article), expected reward linear per action: $\mathbb{E}[r \mid x, a] = x_{t,a}^\top \theta^\star$.

Ridge estimation: $$A_t = \lambda I + \sum_{\tau < t} x_{\tau} x_{\tau}^\top, \qquad b_t = \sum_{\tau < t} x_\tau\, r_\tau, \qquad \hat\theta_t = A_t^{-1} b_t,$$ and index rule (confidence ellipsoid): $$a_t = \arg\max_a\ x_{t,a}^\top \hat\theta_t + \alpha \sqrt{x_{t,a}^\top A_t^{-1} x_{t,a}}.$$

The bonus $\sqrt{x^\top A^{-1} x}$ is the *directional* uncertainty (small in often-observed directions); regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011).

LinUCB (Li et al., 2010) deployed this idea at scale for news article recommendation — the context = user/article features, exactly the schema of modern recommender systems (network variants: NeuralTS, etc.).
:::

::: note
[LinUCB in the team project]{.tag} The same algorithm serves two Year 1 subjects. As a **retrieval router** (Y1.1), the context is a feature vector of the question, the arms are the retrieval modes (none, vector, GraphRAG, agentic) and the reward is answer correctness minus a token cost. As a **cold-start recommender** (Y1.3), the context joins user and article embeddings and the reward is a click.
:::

### 4.1. Exploring beyond bandits

-   **Three families of exploration**: $\varepsilon$-greedy (blind, learns nothing from the structure); optimism (UCB, count-based: bonus $\beta/\sqrt{N(s,a)}$ — explore what is *uncertain*); posterior (Thompson: explore what is *plausible*). In MDPs, optimism yields the UCT/Monte-Carlo Tree Search algorithms (the heart of AlphaGo).
-   **Intrinsic exploration in high dimension**: when the count $N(s,a)$ is empty (states almost all distinct — images), replace novelty by a *prediction error*.

    **RND** (Burda et al., 2019, sketch): a *random frozen* target network $f$ and a predictor $g$ trained to imitate $f$ on visited states; the intrinsic reward $r_{\mathrm{int}}(s) = \|f(s) - g(s)\|_2^2$ is large on *new* states (never seen by $g$) and fades with familiarity — a similarity-based generalization of count-based exploration;
-   **Exploration in LLMs**: RLHF and LLM evaluation (best-of-n, jury voting) are bandit problems (arms = answers, context = prompt).

    RLVR (RL from verifiable rewards) uses exploration for reasoning-chain search (verifiable reward = binomial oracle); policy entropy and sampling temperature play the role of the temperature $\alpha$ of SAC (ch. 6) — a topic taken up again in the M2 Large Language Models module.

### 4.2. Monte-Carlo tree search

The official programme moves from bandits to Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS), and the link is direct: MCTS treats *every node of a search tree as a bandit*. It is a planning method — it needs a simulator of the environment (a game engine, a learned model as in section 6.4) — that spends a budget of simulations from the current state and concentrates them on the promising branches.

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — MCTS: four phases per simulation]{.tag} The tree stores, for each node $s$ and action $a$, a visit count $N(s,a)$ and a mean return $Q(s,a)$; write $N(s) = \sum_a N(s,a)$. Each simulation runs:

1.  **selection** — from the root, descend by choosing in each node the action given by a bandit rule;
2.  **expansion** — on reaching a node with an untried action, add the child;
3.  **evaluation** — estimate the value of the new leaf by a random *rollout* to the end of the game, or by a value network;
4.  **backup** — propagate the obtained return $G$ along the path:
    $$
    N(s,a) \leftarrow N(s,a) + 1, \qquad Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \frac{G - Q(s,a)}{N(s,a)}.
    $$

After the budget is spent, play the most visited root action (more robust than the highest mean).
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.7 — UCT (Kocsis & Szepesvári, 2006)]{.tag} UCT uses the UCB index of Theorem 4.2 as the selection rule, with the node visit count $N(s)$ in place of $t$: $$a = \arg\max_a\ Q(s,a) + c\,\sqrt{\frac{\ln N(s)}{N(s,a)}}.$$

For a finite-horizon problem and a suitable constant $c$, the probability of recommending a suboptimal action at the root tends to zero as the number of simulations grows (consistency), and the bias of the root estimate decreases as $O(\log n / n)$.

The difficulty compared with a bandit: the returns observed at an inner node are *non-stationary*, because the policy below it keeps improving — the analysis handles this drift by induction from the leaves.

**AlphaZero's PUCT** replaces the rollout by a value network $v_\phi$ and biases exploration with a policy network $p_\phi$:
$$
a = \arg\max_a Q(s,a) + c\, p_\phi(a\mid s)\,\frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1 + N(s,a)} ;
$$
the visit distribution at the root then serves as the training target of $p_\phi$ (self-play, section 7.1).
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.8 — One UCT selection step, computed]{.tag} At the root, after $N(s) = 8$ simulations:

-   action $a_1$ has $N = 6$, $Q = 0.5$;
-   action $a_2$ has $N = 2$, $Q = 0.75$.

Take $c = \sqrt 2$, so the bonus is $\sqrt{2 \ln N(s) / N(s,a)}$ with $2\ln 8 \approx 4.159$.

-   Index of $a_1$: $0.5 + \sqrt{4.159/6} \approx 0.5 + 0.833 = 1.333$.
-   Index of $a_2$: $0.75 + \sqrt{4.159/2} \approx 0.75 + 1.442 = 2.192$.

UCT selects $a_2$ — both because its mean is higher and because it is less explored.

Suppose this simulation returns $G = 0$: now $N(a_2) = 3$, $Q(a_2) = 0.5$, $N(s) = 9$ and $2\ln 9 \approx 4.394$. New indices:

-   $a_1$: $0.5 + \sqrt{4.394/6} \approx 1.356$;
-   $a_2$: $0.5 + \sqrt{4.394/3} \approx 1.710$.

Equal means, so the less visited $a_2$ is still preferred; as counts grow the bonuses shrink like $1/\sqrt{N}$ and the means decide.
:::

## 5. Policy gradients, actor-critic and gradient-free policy search {#ch5}

Value-based methods learn $Q$ and act greedily, which requires a maximization over the actions — awkward for continuous actions, and unable to represent a deliberately random policy. Policy gradient methods parameterize the policy $\pi_\theta$ directly and climb the gradient of the expected return $J(\theta)$.

### 5.1. REINFORCE: the proof step by step

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.1 — REINFORCE (Williams, 1992), complete proof]{.tag} Let $\pi_\theta$ be differentiable, $\tau = (S_0, A_0, \dots, S_{T})$ a trajectory of return $G(\tau) = \sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t R_t$, and $J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[G(\tau)]$. Then
$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[\Big(\sum_{t=0}^{T} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t)\Big) G(\tau)\Big].
$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (law of the trajectory).** By the chain rule of probabilities (each transition depends only on $(S_t, A_t)$ — Markov): $$p_\theta(\tau) = \mu(S_0) \prod_{t=0}^{T-1} \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t)\, P(S_{t+1} \mid S_t, A_t).$$

**Step 2 (log-derivative).** We differentiate $J = \int p_\theta(\tau) G(\tau)\, d\tau$ permuting derivative and integral (domination): $$\nabla_\theta J = \int G(\tau)\, \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)\, d\tau = \int p_\theta(\tau)\, G(\tau)\, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\, d\tau,$$ using the identity $\nabla p = p\, \nabla \log p$ — the *log-derivative trick*. This is an expectation under $\pi_\theta$: it can be estimated by Monte-Carlo with trajectories *sampled by the current policy*.

**Step 3 (the dynamics vanish).** $$\log p_\theta(\tau) = \log \mu(S_0) + \sum_t \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t) + \sum_t \log P(S_{t+1} \mid S_t, A_t),$$ and the first and last terms *do not depend on $\theta$*: their gradient is zero. Only the action scores remain: $$\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\Big[G(\tau) \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t)\Big]. \qquad \blacksquare$$

*Reading:* raise the probability of rich trajectories (large $G$), lower the poor ones — the world model is useless, only the actions are accountable.
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Unbiased baseline: demonstration]{.tag} For every function $b : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}$ (not depending on the action): $$\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[b(S_t)\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t)\Big] = 0 \qquad \text{for each } t,$$ so subtracting $b$ does not change $\nabla_\theta J$.

::: proof
Condition on $S_t = s$ (with law $d_t(s)$ under $\pi_\theta$): $$\mathbb{E}\big[b(S_t)\, \nabla \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t)\big] = \sum_s d_t(s)\, b(s) \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s).$$

Now
$$
\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s) = \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a\mid s)
$$
(same identity as in step 2), so the inner sum equals
$$
\nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0.
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

*Variance analysis.* The empirical gradient $(G - b)\nabla\log\pi$ has variance
$$
\mathrm{Var}[G \nabla\log\pi] + \mathrm{Var}[b\nabla\log\pi] - 2\,\mathrm{Cov} :
$$
choosing $b(s)$ close to $\mathbb{E}[G \mid S_t = s]$ makes the covariance maximal and almost cancels the first order.

The optimal *constant* baseline (minimizing the variance of the estimator for a given state) equals
$$
b^\star = \mathbb{E}\big[G \|\nabla \log \pi\|^2\big] / \mathbb{E}\big[\|\nabla \log \pi\|^2\big]
$$
(set to zero the derivative in $b$ of $\mathbb{E}\big[(G - b)^2 \|\nabla \log \pi\|^2\big]$) — and the natural choice $b(s) = V^\pi(s)$ turns $G - b$ into the **advantage** $A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s)$: same expectation, drastically reduced variance.

The policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al. 1999) states the result for the discounted objective $J(\theta)$ of Definition 1.1 with $\pi = \pi_\theta$. It uses the discounted state-visitation distribution of Definition 1.4,
$$
d^\pi(s) = (1-\gamma)\sum_{t \geq 0} \gamma^t\, \mathbb{P}_\pi[S_t = s].
$$

::: key
[Key result — policy gradient theorem]{.tag}
$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\, \mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^\pi,\, a \sim \pi}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, Q^\pi(s,a)\big].
$$
:::

The factor $1/(1-\gamma)$ undoes the normalization of $d^\pi$; $Q^\pi$ replaces the return $G$, and $A^\pi$ can replace $Q^\pi$ (Proposition 5.2).

Implementations usually absorb the factor into the step size and sample states along trajectories without the $\gamma^t$ weights, a small bias accepted in practice.
::::

### 5.2. Actor-critic

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.3 — A2C: semi-gradients]{.tag} Two networks: the **actor** $\pi_\theta$ and the **critic** $V_w$. At each transition: $$\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V_w(S_{t+1}) - V_w(S_t) \quad (\text{TD error, chapter 3}),$$ $$w \leftarrow w + \alpha_w\, \delta_t\, \nabla_w V_w(S_t) \quad (\text{critic: TD(0) semi-gradient}),$$ $$\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha_\theta\, \delta_t\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(A_t \mid S_t) \quad (\text{actor: REINFORCE with } \delta_t \text{ as advantage}).$$ We say *semi*-gradient because the target $V_w(S_{t+1})$ depends on $w$ but is not differentiated (the true gradient of the TD loss would bring the unstable "double sampling" — cf. deadly triad, ch. 3). Two step scales $\alpha_w \gg \alpha_\theta$ (the critic must keep up); the estimated advantage $\hat A_t = \delta_t$ is replaced in practice by GAE (Proposition 3.4). **A3C** (Mnih et al., 2016): parallel actors explore independent environments and push their gradients to a shared parameter — asynchronous hence without replay; **A2C** is its synchronized (batched) variant, simpler and equivalent in performance.
:::

### 5.3. From trust region to PPO

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Natural gradient and TRPO (sketch)]{.tag} The relevant *geometry* on policies is the KL divergence, not the Euclidean distance on $\theta$ (a reparameterization changes the algorithm).

The **natural gradient** corrects this: $\tilde\nabla J = F(\theta)^{-1} \nabla_\theta J$, where
$$
F(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^\pi,\, a \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a \mid s)^\top\big]
$$
is the Fisher matrix.

Kakade & Langford (2002) prove a *monotone improvement*, extended to arbitrary policies by Schulman et al. (2015). The gain $J(\pi') - J(\pi)$ of any new policy $\pi'$ is lower-bounded by the one-step *surrogate* gain
$$
\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\,\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^\pi, a \sim \pi}\Big[ \frac{\pi'(a\mid s)}{\pi(a\mid s)}\, A^\pi(s,a)\Big]
$$
minus a penalty term in
$$
\max_s \mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot\mid s) \,\|\, \pi'(\cdot\mid s)).
$$
The surrogate uses the old distribution $d^\pi$ in place of $d^{\pi'}$, which is why it is faithful only near $\pi$.

**TRPO** (Schulman et al., 2015) maximizes this surrogate over $\pi_\theta$, with $\pi = \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}$, under a trust-region constraint
$$
\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}}}\big[\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(\cdot \mid s) \,\|\, \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s)\big)\big] \leq \delta .
$$
It is solved approximately by a conjugate-gradient computation of the natural-gradient direction followed by a line search — effective but heavy.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — PPO-clip (Schulman et al., 2017): a pessimistic bound of the surrogate]{.tag} With the importance ratio
$$
\rho_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)}
$$
and the advantage $\hat A_t$ (GAE): $$L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\big[\min\big(\rho_t(\theta)\, \hat A_t,\ \ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t(\theta), 1{-}\epsilon, 1{+}\epsilon)\, \hat A_t\big)\big].$$

::: proof
**PPO-clip lower-bounds the importance surrogate** $L^{\mathrm{IS}} = \mathbb{E}[\rho_t \hat A_t]$, point by point:

-   if $\hat A_t > 0$ (good action): the minimum is at most $\rho_t \hat A_t$ trivially, and the clip caps the incentive at $1 + \epsilon$: no motivation to blow up the probability of an already rewarded action;
-   if $\hat A_t < 0$ (bad action):
    -   if $\rho_t \geq 1 - \epsilon$, the min equals $\rho_t \hat A_t$ (equality);
    -   if $\rho_t < 1 - \epsilon$, the min equals $(1-\epsilon)\hat A_t \leq \rho_t \hat A_t$ (since $\hat A_t < 0$ and $1 - \epsilon > \rho_t$): the gradient vanishes — one does not "over-punish" beyond the region.

So $L^{\mathrm{CLIP}} \leq L^{\mathrm{IS}}$: maximizing the *pessimistic* bound of a valid approximation of the true gain (Proposition 5.4) — an improvement of the lower bound cannot destroy the policy, hence the *monotone improvement intuition* without explicit KL constraint or second derivative; the clipping suffices to keep the ratios in the region where the surrogate is faithful. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Implementation details: a few epochs of gradient ascent per batch of trajectories, normalized advantages, entropy bonus, masking of truncated trajectories. PPO is *the* method behind LLM alignment (RLHF/PPO, then GRPO — cf. M2 Large Language Models module, post-training chapter; the importance ratio there is exactly the same object, applied to tokens).
::::

```python
# REINFORCE with baseline skeleton (PyTorch, CartPole problem)
logits = policy_net(states)                 # (B, n_actions)
dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits)
actions = dist.sample()
logp = dist.log_prob(actions)
returns = compute_returns(rewards, gamma)   # G_t
advantage = returns - value_net(states).squeeze(-1)   # learned baseline
loss = -(logp * advantage.detach()).mean() + 0.5 * advantage.pow(2).mean()
optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
# PPO: on a stored batch (states, actions, logp_old, returns, adv_gae), use instead
#   logp = dist.log_prob(actions)                 # stored actions under the current policy
#   ratio = torch.exp(logp - logp_old)            # rho_t(theta); logp_old stored, no gradient
#   adv = adv_gae.detach()                        # precomputed GAE advantages (Prop. 3.4)
#   l1 = ratio * adv; l2 = torch.clamp(ratio, 1-eps, 1+eps) * adv
#   v_loss = (returns - value_net(states).squeeze(-1)).pow(2).mean()   # critic regresses on returns
#   loss = -torch.min(l1, l2).mean() + 0.5 * v_loss - 0.01 * dist.entropy().mean()
```

### 5.4. Gradient-free and evolutionary policy search

The official programme devotes a week to autonomous agents seen as *optimization problems*, with a focus on methods for direct policy search that do not differentiate the policy at all. They treat $\theta \mapsto J(\theta)$ as a black box that can only be evaluated, noisily, by running episodes — which is enough to optimize it.

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.6 — Cross-entropy method (CEM)]{.tag} Keep a Gaussian search distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))$ over policy parameters. At each generation: sample $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_N$; evaluate each by the return of a few episodes; keep the *elite* (the best fraction $\rho$, e.g. $10\%$); refit $\mu$ and $\sigma$ to the elite by maximum likelihood (their mean and standard deviation). The distribution contracts around good regions. CMA-ES refines the idea by adapting a full covariance matrix. CEM is also the standard optimizer of action sequences in model-predictive control (section 6.4).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — Evolution strategies estimate a smoothed gradient]{.tag} Let
$$
J_\sigma(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}[J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon)]
$$
be the Gaussian-smoothed objective. Then
$$
\nabla_\theta J_\sigma(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sigma}\, \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\big[J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon)\, \varepsilon\big],
$$
estimated by
$$
\frac{1}{N\sigma}\sum_i J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon_i)\,\varepsilon_i ,
$$
with no derivative of $J$ (Salimans et al., 2017).

::: proof
Write $x = \theta + \sigma\varepsilon$, so $x \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2 I)$ with density
$$
\varphi_\theta(x) \propto \exp(-\|x - \theta\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)
$$
and $J_\sigma(\theta) = \int J(x)\,\varphi_\theta(x)\,dx$.

Differentiate under the integral and use the log-derivative trick of Theorem 5.1:
$$
\nabla_\theta \varphi_\theta(x) = \varphi_\theta(x)\,\nabla_\theta \log\varphi_\theta(x) = \varphi_\theta(x)\,\frac{x - \theta}{\sigma^2}.
$$
Hence
$$
\nabla_\theta J_\sigma = \mathbb{E}\big[J(x)\,\frac{x - \theta}{\sigma^2}\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon)\,\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\big].
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

*Reading:* REINFORCE perturbs the *actions* and differentiates their log-probability; ES perturbs the *parameters* and differentiates the log-density of the search distribution — the same identity, applied in parameter space.

Subtracting a baseline (Proposition 5.2) and using antithetic pairs $\pm\varepsilon_i$ reduce the variance. ES needs no backpropagation and is indifferent to long delays between action and reward; workers only exchange scalar returns, so it parallelizes over thousands of CPUs. Its price is a sample cost that grows with the dimension of $\theta$.
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.8 — The ES gradient on a quadratic]{.tag} Take $J(\theta) = -(\theta - 3)^2$ in one dimension. Expanding,
$$
J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon) = -(\theta - 3)^2 - 2\sigma(\theta - 3)\varepsilon - \sigma^2\varepsilon^2 .
$$
Multiply by $\varepsilon$ and take expectations with
$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^3] = 0, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] = 1 :
$$
$$
\mathbb{E}[J(\theta + \sigma\varepsilon)\varepsilon] = -2\sigma(\theta - 3),
$$
so the ES gradient equals $-2(\theta - 3)$, the exact derivative, whatever $\sigma$.

Here $J_\sigma = J - \sigma^2$ differs from $J$ by a constant; on a rugged objective, smoothing with a larger $\sigma$ really changes the landscape and helps jump over narrow local optima.
:::

::: note
[Other optimization settings named by the programme]{.tag}

-   **Stochastic**: $J$ is only observed through noisy returns — every method of this course lives there.
-   **Multi-objective**: the return is a vector $J(\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ (speed and energy, reward and safety); $\theta$ *dominates* $\theta'$ if it is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one, and the goal is the **Pareto front** of non-dominated policies. A linear scalarization $w^\top J$ only reaches the convex part of that front, which is why evolutionary algorithms that keep a whole population (NSGA-II) are popular here.
-   **Multimodal**: $J$ has several local optima; population methods and the Gaussian smoothing of Example 5.8 explore several basins at once, where a single gradient ascent stays in the first one.
-   **Constrained**: maximize the return under a cost budget — the constrained MDP of section 6.2.
-   **Dynamic**: the objective drifts over time, the setting of section 8.2.
:::

::: note
[Architecture search as policy search]{.tag} The programme also mentions architecture search.

In Zoph & Le (2017), a recurrent *controller* emits an architecture token by token (layer types, widths); the reward is the validation accuracy of the trained child network, and the controller is updated with REINFORCE (Theorem 5.1) — a one-step episode with a discrete action sequence. Real et al. (2019) obtained comparable architectures with a simple evolutionary method (regularized evolution), the gradient-free counterpart above. Both show that "search over designs" is a sequential decision problem.
:::

### 5.5. Neural combinatorial optimisation: routing as policy search

Logistics problems — vehicle routing, dispatch, scheduling — are combinatorial: a solution is a sequence of discrete choices. Building it is therefore a one-episode MDP, and a policy network trained by REINFORCE becomes a fast heuristic solver that generalizes across instances.

::: def
[Definition 5.9 — Constructive policy for the travelling salesman problem]{.tag} An instance is a set of $n$ cities $x_1, \dots, x_n \in [0,1]^2$. A policy builds a tour $\pi = (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_n)$ one city at a time, the cities already visited being masked out:
$$
p_\theta(\pi \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_\theta(\pi_t \mid x, \pi_{<t}).
$$
The state is the partial tour, the action the next city, and the cost is the tour length
$$
L(\pi) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \|x_{\pi_{t+1}} - x_{\pi_t}\|_2, \qquad \pi_{n+1} = \pi_1 .
$$

In the **Attention Model** (Kool, van Hoof & Welling, 2019), a transformer encoder without positional encoding embeds the cities — the instance is a set, so the encoder is permutation-equivariant — and a decoder attends from the current context (graph embedding, first and last city) to the unvisited cities.
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.10 — REINFORCE with a greedy-rollout baseline (Kool et al., 2019)]{.tag} For a batch of random instances, sample tours $\pi \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)$ and descend the gradient of the expected length (Theorem 5.1 with a one-step episode):
$$
\nabla_\theta\, \mathbb{E}_{\pi \sim p_\theta}[L(\pi)] = \mathbb{E}\big[(L(\pi) - b(x))\, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\pi \mid x)\big].
$$
The baseline $b(x)$ is the length of the greedy tour decoded by a frozen copy of the best policy so far; the copy is replaced when a paired t-test on fresh instances shows a significant improvement.

The baseline depends on the instance, not on the sampled tour, so the gradient stays unbiased (Proposition 5.2): a tour is reinforced when it beats the policy's own greedy answer on the same instance.
:::

**POMO** (Kwon et al., 2020) exploits a symmetry of the TSP: a tour can start from any of its $n$ cities. It samples $N = n$ tours per instance, each forced to start at a different city, and uses their mean length as a shared baseline.

This baseline needs no extra rollout. Since the $N$ tours are sampled independently, it only rescales the expected gradient by $(N-1)/N$.

The same estimator, with capacities and time windows added to the mask, trains vehicle-routing policies: this is the entry point for the fleet-dispatch subject (Y1.2) and the language-driven dispatcher of Year 2. Exercise 17 trains a TSP-20 policy.

## 6. Deep RL and advanced methods: DQN, continuous control, offline, distributional, model-based, imitation {#ch6}

The tabular methods of ch. 3 store one value per state-action pair, which is impossible for Atari screens or robot joints. Deep RL replaces the table by a neural network — and thereby meets the deadly triad of ch. 3.

This chapter presents the stabilizers that make it work, the extensions to continuous actions, and learning from a fixed dataset; sections 6.3–6.6 then cover the advanced families named by the official programme: distributional RL, model-based RL and planning, imitation and inverse RL, and decision transformers.

Several of these methods, and the RLHF of the LLM course, regularize a policy toward a reference one. One lemma gives their optimum over unrestricted policies; we state it once here.

:::: {#kl-lemma .thm}
[Lemma — KL-regularised policy improvement]{.tag} Let $\pi_0$ be a reference distribution over actions (or answers) $a$, $r$ a bounded reward and $\beta > 0$. Over all distributions $\pi$, the problem
$$
\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[r(a)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_0)
$$
has the unique solution
$$
\pi^\star(a) = \frac{\pi_0(a)\, e^{r(a)/\beta}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_a \pi_0(a)\, e^{r(a)/\beta},
$$
and its optimal value is $\beta \log Z$.

::: proof
Take $\pi$ with $\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_0) < \infty$. Taking logarithms in the definition of $\pi^\star$ gives
$$
r = \beta \log\frac{\pi^\star}{\pi_0} + \beta \log Z .
$$
Substituting,
$$
\mathbb{E}_\pi[r] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_0) = \beta\,\mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\log\frac{\pi^\star}{\pi_0} - \log\frac{\pi}{\pi_0}\Big] + \beta\log Z = \beta\log Z - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^\star).
$$
By Gibbs' inequality, the KL divergence is nonnegative and vanishes only at $\pi = \pi^\star$ ([Machine Learning, Proposition 0.8](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#entropy-kl)). The maximum is therefore $\beta\log Z$, reached only at $\pi^\star$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Two readings of the lemma recur across the program.

-   **SAC** (Algorithm 6.4) takes $\pi_0$ uniform over $\mathcal{A}$ and $\beta = \alpha$. Since the KL to the uniform policy is $\log|\mathcal{A}| - \mathcal{H}(\pi)$, the entropy bonus is a KL penalty, and the optimum is the softmax $\pi^\star \propto e^{Q/\alpha}$.
-   **RLHF** takes $\pi_0 = \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $r = r_\phi(x, \cdot)$, which gives $\pi^\star \propto \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} e^{r_\phi/\beta}$: step 1 of the DPO derivation.

This is the canonical statement of the lemma on the site: [Large Language Models, ch. 5](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch5) and [Control in Generative AI, ch. 5](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html#ch5) (Theorem 5.1) recall it.
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.1 — DQN (Mnih et al., 2015)]{.tag} Q-learning where $Q(s, a; \theta)$ is a network; stabilized by:

-   **experience replay**: resampling past transitions (breaks the temporal correlation and approaches the i.i.d. assumption of SGD);
-   **target network** $\theta^-$ frozen and periodically synchronized: target $y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-)$ (avoids chasing a moving target — the deadly triad, ch. 3);
-   loss $\big(y - Q(s, a; \theta)\big)^2$.
:::

```python
# Minimal DQN (PyTorch) -- the three stabilizers in evidence
replay = deque(maxlen=100_000)            # 1. experience replay
def train_step(batch=128, gamma=0.99):
    s, a, r, s2, done = sample(replay, batch)
    with torch.no_grad():                 # 2. target network (frozen theta^-)
        y = r + gamma * (1 - done) * target_net(s2).max(1).values
    q = policy_net(s).gather(1, a).squeeze(1)
    loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(q, y)         # 3. TD loss (Huber, more robust)
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(policy_net.parameters(), 10)
    optimizer.step()
# Double DQN (algorithm 3.6): replace the 'y' line with
#   a2 = policy_net(s2).argmax(1, keepdim=True)          # selection: current network
#   y = r + gamma * (1 - done) * target_net(s2).gather(1, a2).squeeze(1)  # evaluation: target
```

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.2 — Rainbow (Hessel et al., 2018): six ingredients]{.tag} Rainbow combines six independent improvements of DQN, each attacking a precise weakness:

| Ingredient | Idea | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Double Q-learning | decouple selection/evaluation (Algorithm 3.6) | overestimation bias (Th. 3.5) |
| Prioritized replay | sample transitions proportionally to the TD error $|\delta|$ | uniform replay |
| Dueling architecture | two heads $V(s)$ and $A(s,a)$, recombined $Q = V + A - \mathrm{avg}_a A$ | similar actions, state/value generalization |
| Multi-step (n-step) | target with the $G^{(n)}$ return (Def. 3.3), typically $n=3$ | slow reward propagation |
| Distributional (C51) | predict the *distribution* of $Z(s,a)$ over 51 atoms, projected cross-entropy | signal variance, richer learning |
| Noisy nets | noisy biases/weights, explored by the learned noise itself | crude $\varepsilon$-greedy |

Rainbow's main contribution is to show that the gains *compose*: on the 57 Atari games, the combination matches the final performance of DQN after about 7M frames (DQN was trained for 200M) and outperforms every individual variant within 44M frames.
:::

::: def
[Prioritized experience replay and its bias correction]{.tag} Uniform replay wastes updates on transitions the network already predicts well. Prioritized replay (Schaul et al., 2016) samples transition $i$ with probability
$$
P(i) = \frac{p_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_k p_k^{\alpha}}, \qquad p_i = |\delta_i| + \epsilon,
$$
where $\delta_i$ is its last TD error and $\alpha \in [0,1]$ interpolates between uniform ($\alpha = 0$) and greedy prioritization.

Sampling non-uniformly changes the distribution the loss is averaged over, which biases the fixed point; the correction is an importance weight (Proposition 0.9)
$$
w_i = \big(N\,P(i)\big)^{-\beta} / \max_j w_j
$$
multiplying the loss of transition $i$, with $\beta$ annealed to $1$ by the end of training, when unbiasedness matters most.

Priorities are updated with the new $|\delta_i|$ after each use; a sum-tree gives $O(\log N)$ sampling.
:::

### 6.1. Continuous actions: DDPG and SAC

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.3 — DDPG (Lillicrap et al., 2016)]{.tag} The $\max_a$ is impossible in continuous spaces; DDPG learns *two* networks: a critic $Q_w(s,a)$ and a *deterministic* actor $\mu_\theta(s)$ trained by the *deterministic policy gradient*
$$
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_a Q_w(s, a)\big|_{a = \mu_\theta(s)}\, \nabla_\theta \mu_\theta(s)\big]
$$
— the max of Q-learning is replaced by gradient ascent of $Q$ through the actor.

Off-policy (replay + targets), but fragile: the $Q$/actor pair can settle on erroneous maxima of $Q$ (overestimation, again); TD3 adds double Q and noisy targets.
:::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 6.4 — SAC: maximum entropy, derivation]{.tag} SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) maximizes the return *and* the entropy: $$J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_t \gamma^t \big(r_t + \alpha\, \mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot \mid S_t))\big)\Big], \qquad \mathcal{H}(\pi) = -\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[\log \pi(a \mid s)].$$

::: proof
**Optimal softmax policy.** For a fixed $Q$, let us maximize
$$
F(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[Q(s,a)] + \alpha \mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot\mid s))
$$
over distributions. Set $\pi^\star(a\mid s) \propto \exp(Q(s,a)/\alpha)$, with normalization constant $Z(s) = \sum_a e^{Q(s,a)/\alpha}$. Then: $$F(\pi) = -\alpha\, \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\log \frac{\pi(a\mid s)}{\pi^\star(a\mid s)}\Big] + \alpha \log Z(s) = -\alpha\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^\star) + \alpha\log Z(s),$$ (identification by expanding $\log \pi^\star = Q/\alpha - \log Z$).

The unique maximum is attained at $\pi = \pi^\star$, with value $\alpha \log Z(s)$: the optimal policy weights the actions by a **softmax of temperature $\alpha$** of the Q-values — exploring is literally optimal in this criterion. This is the KL-regularised lemma that opens the chapter, with a uniform $\pi_0$ and $\beta = \alpha$.

**"Soft" Bellman operator.** The target equation becomes
$$
Q^\star(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'}[V(s')]
$$
with the *soft value*
$$
V(s') = \alpha \log \sum_{a'} e^{Q(s',a')/\alpha}
$$
— the max is replaced by a log-sum-exp of temperature $\alpha$; the log-sum-exp is 1-Lipschitz for $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, so $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{soft}}$ remains a $\gamma$-contraction: the whole theory of chapter 1 survives. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Auto-learned temperature $\alpha$.** $\alpha$ tunes the exploration/exploitation trade-off; SAC treats it by a Lagrangian: minimize
$$
J(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}[-\alpha \log \pi(a\mid s)] - \alpha\, \bar{\mathcal{H}},
$$
where $\bar{\mathcal{H}}$ is the target entropy: $\alpha$ rises when the actual entropy falls below the target (forced exploration), falls otherwise.

Implementation: three networks (actor + two critics, min against overestimation), reparameterization to backpropagate through sampling, and no GAE (off-policy, one-step targets). SAC is the standard for continuous environments (robotics, control).
::::

### 6.2. Offline RL and sim-to-real

::: prop
[Offline RL (batch learning): the distribution shift]{.tag} Data: a fixed dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of transitions (teleoperator, logs, simulator); no interaction. The danger: $Q$ is evaluated on *out-of-distribution* actions (never tried in $\mathcal{D}$); the $\max_{a'}$ of Q-learning queries the network where it has seen nothing — uncorrected overestimation (Theorem 3.5, aggravated).
